newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf Arab leaders congratulate Iran's Khatami.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arab leaders congratulate Iran's Khatami.

text.p: Leaders of Gulf Arab states, which view the government of their neighbour Iran with suspicion, on Sunday congratulated Iran's moderate president-elect Mohammad Khatami on his stunning election victory.

Official Gulf news agencies said the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman congratulated Khatami on his victory, the biggest political upset since the 1979 Islamic revolution.

Iran is trying to improve ties with Gulf Arab states, which have accused its government of interfering in their internal affairs -- a charge Iran denies -- and voiced concern over its armament programme.
Saudi King Fahd, in a message to Khatami on Saturday night, congratulated him on "the trust that the Iranian people have shown in you, wishing you success in the service of your country and people."
The official Saudi Press Agency said King Fahd expressed a desire to "strengthen the good relations between our brotherly countries in the service of our Islamic cause."
Khatami, a moderate former culture minister, was elected president on Saturday in an upset victory over the Islamic republic's conservative establishment.
Khatami will take over in August from President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down after completing the maximum two four-year terms permitted by law.

Relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran -- two of the world's top oil producers -- have often been tense since Iran's 1979 Islamic revolution, mainly over the presence of Western forces in the Gulf, the annual Moslem pilgrimage to Mecca, Iran's armament programme and charges that Iran interfered in the internal affairs of its neighbours.
In the United Arab Emirates -- locked in a territorial dispute with Iran -- the Gulf Today newspaper called on Khatami to improve ties with Iran's Arab neighbours.

"His efforts to improve Iran's international relations should...be aimed not only at the West and a few of the bigger developing economies, but also closer to home," the English-language daily said in an editorial.
